title: Iranian Duo Charged in Alleged Plot Against UK Jewish Community, Al Jazeera Reports
body:
British prosecutors on Friday announced that two Iranian nationals have been formally charged with conspiring to mount a terrorist attack against the Jewish community in Manchester, an operation allegedly planned to take place on or before the Jewish holy day of Yom Kippur. The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said the men, identified as Rahman Salahi and Mohammad Al‑Fazeli, were accused of preparing a “serious violent offence” that would have targeted a synagogue or other Jewish gathering in the city, potentially endangering hundreds of worshippers. The indictment marks the latest high‑profile case linking foreign‑state actors to extremist plots on British soil and underscores the heightened vigilance of security services during the volatile period surrounding the Israel‑Hamas conflict.

According to the CPS, the pair allegedly began coordinating the plot in early 2024 after being radicalised through online propaganda that framed the Israel‑Palestine war as a religious duty. Investigators say Salahi and Al‑Fazeli sought to acquire explosives, firearms and other weaponry, and attempted to recruit additional operatives through encrypted messaging apps. Their communications, intercepted by the National Crime Agency (NCA) and MI5, revealed a clear intent to strike a Jewish place of worship during Yom Kippur, a day when congregants would be gathered for the most solemn services of the Jewish calendar. The alleged timing would have maximised casualties and amplified the psychological impact of the attack.

The case arrives at a moment when the United Kingdom is grappling with a surge in hate‑motivated incidents linked to the ongoing Gaza war. Police data released earlier this year showed a 70 percent rise in anti‑Jewish offences compared with pre‑conflict levels, prompting community leaders to call for stronger protective measures. In Manchester, a city with a vibrant and historic Jewish population, local authorities have already heightened security around synagogues, schools and community centres. The charges against Salahi and Al‑Fazeli are being presented as evidence that the UK’s counter‑terrorism apparatus is capable of intercepting threats before they materialise, even when the conspirators are allegedly acting on behalf of a foreign government.

Both defendants are reported to have Iranian citizenship and are believed to have travelled to the United Kingdom on student visas. While the CPS has not formally linked the alleged plot to the Iranian state, British officials have repeatedly warned that Tehran’s support for extremist groups poses a “significant and persistent” threat to national security. In recent years, Iranian‑linked networks have been implicated in a series of plots across Europe, ranging from attempted bombings to the procurement of chemical weapons. The current indictment therefore adds to a growing dossier of Iran‑sponsored or inspired terrorism that has strained diplomatic relations between London and Tehran.

Legal experts note that the prosecution will need to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the two men took concrete steps towards executing the attack, not merely that they entertained extremist ideas. The CPS has indicated that evidence includes seized materials, digital footprints and testimonies from undercover officers who infiltrated the suspects’ communications. If convicted, Salahi and Al‑Fazeli could face life imprisonment under the UK’s Terrorism Act, reflecting the seriousness with which the judiciary treats plots targeting religious minorities.

Looking ahead, the case is expected to serve as a litmus test for Britain’s ability to deter foreign‑backed terrorism while safeguarding civil liberties. Security agencies have signalled that surveillance and community‑engagement initiatives will be intensified, particularly in university towns where radicalisation pathways often begin. Meanwhile, Jewish organisations across the country are urging authorities to maintain robust protection during the upcoming high‑holiday season, which includes Passover and the summer festivals. The outcome of the trial will likely influence both policy and public perception of how effectively the UK can counteract transnational extremist threats in an increasingly volatile geopolitical climate.
